Mores are the deeply held moral beliefs, values, and unwritten rules that a society or group considers absolutely essential to its way of life. They are not just habits or preferences — they are the standards a community treats as non-negotiable, the things people feel in their gut are fundamentally right or wrong.

Think of mores as the invisible moral backbone of a society. They tell people not just how things are done, but how things must be done — and more importantly, what is simply unacceptable.

Every society has many kinds of rules. Some are written into law. Some are casual habits. But mores sit in a very specific place: they are unwritten, yet they carry enormous moral weight. People follow mores not because a law forces them to, but because violating them feels deeply wrong — almost like a betrayal of what it means to be a decent human being in that community.

Here are a few things that make mores unique:

1. They are moral, not just social.
Mores are not just about politeness or convenience. They are connected to a community's deepest sense of right and wrong. Violating them doesn't just make you rude — it makes you bad. Other people don't just feel uncomfortable; they feel genuinely offended, outraged, or disgusted.

2. They are enforced by society, not the law.
Mores are policed by the community itself — through social pressure, disapproval, shame, exclusion, gossip, or outrage. If you break a more, people may stop associating with you, judge you publicly, or treat you as a moral failure. You don't get arrested, but you do get condemned.

3. They are widely shared within a group.
Mores are not just one person's opinion. They represent a broad, shared moral consensus within a community. Most members of the group hold them without even consciously thinking about them. They feel like common sense or basic decency.

4. They feel natural and obvious — but aren't universal.
People living inside a set of mores often assume they are simply "the right way to live." But mores vary significantly across cultures, religions, and historical periods. What one society treats as a moral violation, another may see as completely normal.
How Mores Differ From Similar Things

To truly understand mores, it helps to compare them to related concepts:

Mores vs. Laws
Laws are formal, written rules enforced by a government with official penalties (fines, imprisonment). Mores are informal, unwritten, and enforced by social pressure. Sometimes mores and laws overlap — for example, laws against murder exist partly because killing is also a deeply held more. But not everything illegal violates mores, and not everything that violates mores is illegal.

Mores vs. Folkways
Folkways are the everyday customs and habits of a society — things like how to greet someone, what to wear to a wedding, or which side of the sidewalk to walk on. Breaking a folkway makes you seem odd or impolite. Breaking a more makes you seem morally wrong. The stakes are much higher with mores. The disapproval is not mild annoyance — it is genuine moral condemnation.

Mores vs. Personal Values
Personal values are what you individually believe. Mores are what the collective group believes. Of course, your personal values are often shaped by the mores of the society you grew up in — but the key distinction is that mores belong to the group, not the individual.

• In most societies, there is a strong more against harming children. It's not just illegal — it feels profoundly, viscerally wrong to almost everyone. A person who hurts a child isn't just breaking a rule; they are seen as a moral monster.
  • In many cultures, there is a more around honoring and caring for elderly parents. A person who completely abandons their aging parents isn't arrested, but they may face intense community shame and judgment.
  • Historically, many societies had strong mores around marriage — defining who could marry whom, what counted as fidelity, and what sexual behavior was acceptable. These mores varied dramatically across cultures and time periods.
  • In a workplace culture, there may be a more that the boss should not humiliate employees in public. It may not be written in any handbook, but everyone knows it's deeply wrong, and a manager who does it will face serious social consequences within the organization.
An Important Note: Mores Can Be Wrong

Mores feel like absolute moral truth to the people who hold them — but history shows clearly that they can be deeply mistaken. Many societies have held mores that we now recognize as unjust or cruel: mores that enforced racial separation, excluded women from public life, or condemned people for who they loved. These felt like moral common sense to those communities at the time.

This is one of the most important things to understand about mores: their power comes from how obvious and natural they feel, not from whether they are actually correct. They can be challenged, changed, and overturned — and throughout history, they have been.

Mores are not fixed forever. They evolve slowly, usually driven by:

  • Generational shifts — younger generations often challenge the mores they inherited
  • Social movements — organized efforts to change what a society considers right or wrong
  • Contact with other cultures — exposure to different ways of living can loosen the grip of existing mores
  • Major events — wars, crises, or dramatic social changes can reshape moral consensus

The process is usually slow and often painful, because people who hold a set of mores often experience challenges to them as a personal attack on decency itself.

Mores are the unwritten moral rules that a society treats as absolutely fundamental to right and wrong — enforced not by law, but by powerful social pressure, shared deeply across the community, and felt almost as instinctively as common sense.
